newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Costello pushes for Australian tax reform.
newsitem.headline: Costello pushes for Australian tax reform.

text.p: Australian Treasurer Peter Costello has used Tuesday's High Court decision declaring some state taxes as invalid as a platform to launch a strong government push for the reform of Australia's taxation system.

He told a news conference detailing measures to protect state revenues following a High Court decision on state taxation that the tax system would not last into the next century and reform of the indirect tax system was required.
"Our government wants tax reform. We want to reform the indirect tax system and we are working towards that aim," Costello said.

The High Court ruled on Tuesday that A$5 billion in state franchise fees levied on tobacco, alcohol and petrol were in fact excise taxes, which are reserved for the federal government, and thus were constitutionally invalid.

Costello announced that, at the request of the states, the Australian government would implement from midnight on Wednesday federal taxes to replace the previous state taxes, thereby protecting state revenue bases.
However, he made it clear he did not regard the measure as a permanent solution to the tax problem.
"I don't regard this as a permenant solution to the complexities of the Australian taxation system," he said.
"I think we need to reform our indirect tax system, and I support a reform of our indirect system and I think that that's going to be a much longer term solution."
The need for that reform was great, as the present system was not adequate for the challenges of the new century, he said.
"It's lasting, but it's creaking, it's becoming more and more cumbersome and what that means is we've got work on improving and reforming it," Costello said of the currrent taxation system.

"It will last to the end of the decade, but I wouldn't give the current system a long life expectancy in the next century." Taxation reform, which is generally considered to include a consumption based goods and services tax (GST), has been a difficult politicial topic in recent years.
The Liberal-National coalition went to the 1993 election promising to introduce a GST. It was defeated by the Labor Party, which mounted a negative campaign against the GST.
The coalition then dropped the GST as a policy, and in the lead up to the 1996 elections said it would not be looking to introduce a GST in its first term if it won government.
However, after winning the 1996 election, the coalition has raised the prospect of tax reform, which is seen as most likely to occur after the next election, due by mid 1999.
Costello avoided directly mentioning a GST on Wednesday, although he did stress the need for indirect tax reform.

Costello also said the need for tax reform was being recognised by more sections of the community, but that reform was being blocked by the main opposition party, the Labor Party, He seized on comments by the Labor Premier of New South Wales, Bob Carr, who had earlier on Wednesday spoken of the need for tax reform after the High Court decision.
"Premier Carr is right," Costello said, saying carry supported the government's position.
"The odd man out is the federal Labor Party," he said adding that Labor opposed tax reform for populist reasons.
"If the Federal labor party would be responsible and would join us in getting a modernised Australian taxation system, it would be done in a much more unified way," Costello said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
